claims.text: Premelting and melting behavior in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is primarily governed by particle-size-dependent surface segregation.
Smaller Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles exhibit enhanced surface segregation relative to larger nanoparticles.
Cu and Co are comparatively lower-melting-point elements in this alloy system.
Cu and Co preferentially segregate toward the surfaces of smaller Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Surface segregation produces localized compositional demixing at the nanoparticle surface.
The higher surface-to-volume ratio of smaller nanoparticles promotes surface segregation.
Surface segregation creates a compositionally enriched shell.
The compositionally enriched shell reduces the effective cohesive energy at the nanoparticle surface.
Reduced effective surface cohesive energy facilitates earlier melting.
Larger nanoparticles retain bulk-like chemical homogeneity for longer during heating.
Smaller nanoparticles have a lower melting-onset temperature than larger nanoparticles under otherwise identical heating conditions.
Smaller nanoparticles undergo a more gradual premelting transition than larger nanoparticles.
A liquid-like atomic fraction emerges at the surface earlier in smaller nanoparticles than in larger nanoparticles.
Larger baseline nanoparticles display less pronounced surface segregation and a higher melting-onset temperature.
Surface-segregation effects should dominate the thermal response at particle diameters below approximately 10 nm.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to substantially larger particles or bulk materials.
The melting-onset shift and degree of segregation depend on exact composition, heating rate, and simulation parameters.
The effects of five-element mixing enthalpy on segregation kinetics and liquid-like surface-layer stability remain insufficiently characterized.
